description: Two-person team, Vaishal and Parthiv, focused on shipping real products. Vaishal is a 16-year-old AI/full-stack dev who's built VGT (1,400+ ONNX models on Hugging Face) and Zyrin (earthquake app at GITEX). Building a web tool to visualize SPHEREx sky imagery.
summary:
StellarScope turns NASA’s brand-new SPHEREx Data Release 1, a 102-colour infrared map of the entire sky, into a universe anyone can explore and help investigate. Users stand inside a real-time 3D sky that streams real SPHEREx imagery, with the archive’s own grid of sky tiles laid over it. Clicking any tile shows its real observations, calibrated spectra and raw science files.

At its core is Spectral Scout, our custom AI model. It builds a 4-epoch, 102-channel picture of any region from real SPHEREx exposures, picks the best channels to look at, and flags spectral anomalies and moving objects. Every flag comes with its evidence.

An assistant powered by MBZUAI’s K2 model and NVIDIA’s Nemotron knows the whole platform and can operate it on command. Community missions turn findings into peer-verified contributions. SPHEREx’s data is huge and complex; StellarScope makes it accessible to students and citizen scientists without lowering scientific standards.
details:
What it does

StellarScope is a complete citizen-science platform built on SPHEREx DR1. It works with live data from NASA/IPAC’s archive (IRSA), not static images.

3D sky explorer. You view the sky from its centre, like a planetarium, built with Three.js.

Imagery streams live from the archive, with sharper detail loading as you zoom.

The tile grid is the archive’s own (HEALPix). Our implementation exactly reproduces the official tile positions and footprints, and 19 automated tests check it.

You can switch between any of the 102 wavelengths (0.75–5 µm) or blend three into a false-colour image.

Constellations, star names, sky grids, the ecliptic and the galactic plane can be toggled, Selecting a tile shows:

its real observation history from IRSA (exposures, visits and survey epochs);

calibrated 102-channel spectra and the raw image, coverage-count and quality-flag layers;

the exact sky position of any pixel.

Each science file is about 320 MB, so we read only the bytes needed (about 1 MB at a time). It runs in a browser.

Spectral Scout, our custom SI model (about 129,000 parameters, run in the browser).

The problem: a human can’t scan 102 channels × many epochs × 12,288 tiles.

The input: on demand, our server builds the model’s input from real SPHEREx exposures, not the pre-combined map. It works out exactly which detector pixels cover the target and which wavelength each one sees, fetches only those pixels (about 60 KB per exposure instead of 65 MB), and arranges them into a 4-epoch × 102-channel × 64×64 stack at the instrument’s native 6.15″ pixel scale.

The outputs: a usefulness weight for each channel, with a “View” button that switches the sky to the model’s best channel; spectral anomaly scores; how likely the source is to be moving, with its rate and positions; artefact probabilities (cosmic ray, ghost, persistence and others); and whether the data is complete enough to trust.

Built for honesty: thresholds come from the model card, every score is shown next to its measured evidence (channel, epoch, signal-to-noise), and every result is labelled a candidate for human review.

Tested on real data: on tile 445 it used 40 of 102 channels across 3 epochs, chose 2.79 µm as the best view and raised no false flags, in about 1.4 s.

SI assistant that knows and controls the app.

It’s powered by MBZUAI’s K2 Horizon (via the IFM API) and NVIDIA Nemotron, alternating between them to stay under rate limits, with automatic failover. API keys never leave the server.

It uses real tools instead of making things up: object name lookup via CDS Sesame, live SPHEREx coverage queries, tile geometry and platform stats.

It can operate the interface: fly to objects, select tiles, change wavelengths, toggle layers, run Spectral Scout and navigate pages.

Example: “Show me the Orion Nebula at 3.3 µm” flies there and switches to that channel.

Missions and community.

Guided quests (brown dwarfs, variable stars, interstellar ices, spectral anomalies, Barnard’s Star’s motion, Planet Nine coverage) run from briefing through a submission that carries its evidence.

Peer review: a finding is verified only after two independent reviews, authors can’t review their own work, and a challenge must state its evidence.

Users can claim tiles so no one duplicates work. XP and the leaderboard reward verified work, not clicks.

Planet Nine is framed as a rigorous coverage check against real exposures, never a detection claim.

Learning and polish. Nine interactive lessons use live data. There’s an intro film, a first-visit tour, a personal lab with JSON export of your work, and a settings page.

Benefits and impact: StellarScope gives anyone direct access to calibrated SPHEREx data days after DR1. StellarScope's SI helps people triage regions without overstating results, and its missions produce reproducible contributions that scientists can audit.

Creativity: a planetarium-like experience on real archive data, a custom model fed by live per-exposure cutouts, and an assistant that operates the interface itself.

What we considered: scientific accuracy (validated against official IRSA data), honest SI wording, API key security and rate limiting, accessibility for beginners, and performance (only the bytes needed, cached results).

Tools: TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Three.js/WebGL, Tailwind CSS, Motion, shadcn/ui, Aceternity UI, Astryx, SQLite, ONNX Runtime Web, Python/PyTorch (model training), Vitest, FFmpeg.

We plan to continuously improve the platform as well as our custom SI model to help the public explore sphereX data with ease.

Limitations: With just 2 days of development time some backend features remain eccentric and we aim to fix it in the future.
